title: Introduction to Computer Architecture and Computer Design
subtitle: What is inside a computer, how a program becomes instructions, and who decides how it is all built?
objectives: Explain what computer architecture is and how it differs from computer organization
Name the main components of a computer and how the buses connect them
Trace a program from high-level code to machine instructions, and the steps the CPU takes to execute one
Name the four design goals: performance, cost, power and reliability
Explain what a computer architect designs and why the work matters

steps.question: You tap *Send*. A moment later a friend's phone buzzes. How many different pieces of hardware had to cooperate?
clues: Your touch screen, a processor, memory, a radio chip and storage all took part.
Every one of them was designed to fit together, like an orchestra.
Someone decided what each part does and how the parts talk. That job is **computer architecture**.

notes.explain: Let students name the parts before you reveal the clues. Do not define architecture yet.
notes.ask: What is the most important part of a phone, and what would stop working without the others?

notes.explain: Read the four objectives aloud. Tell students they will see them again in the learning report.

steps.title: Architecture versus organization

left.title: Computer architecture
items: Instruction set, data types, addressing modes

right.title: Computer organization
items: How those features are **built in hardware**

steps.why: Companies can ship a new, faster chip (new organization) that still runs your old programs (same architecture).

explainAgain.beginner: Architecture is the list of things the computer promises to do. Organization is the way the hardware keeps that promise.
explainAgain.technical: Architecture is the programmer-visible interface: the instruction set, registers, data types and addressing modes. Organization (microarchitecture) is the hardware that implements it: datapaths, control logic, caches and buses.
explainAgain.analogy: Two cars with the same pedals and steering wheel but different engines.

deeper.text: The same instruction set (for example x86-64 or ARM) can be implemented by many different organizations across chip generations, which is why old software keeps working on new hardware.

notes.explain: Stress that this split is the single most important idea of the course.
misconceptions: Students treat the two words as synonyms.
notes.ask: If a new chip adds a bigger cache, did the architecture change?

steps.real: Intel and AMD laptops both use the x86-64 instruction set, so the same Windows program runs on either, even though the chips are built differently inside. iPhones and Apple laptops share the Arm instruction set in the same way.

mistake.wrong: Architecture and organization mean the same thing.
mistake.right: Architecture is what the programmer sees. Organization is how the hardware builds it.
mistake.why: Two chips can share an architecture and still be organized very differently.

steps.title: A car analogy
steps.why: It explains why you can upgrade your phone and still run the same apps.

steps.question: Whether a computer has a *multiply* instruction is a decision about…
steps.why: An instruction the programmer can use is part of the architecture.
feedback: Organization decides *how* multiply is carried out inside (a dedicated circuit, or repeated addition). Having the instruction is architecture.
Packaging is the physical housing of the chip.

steps.statement: Two processors from different companies can have different internal designs and still run the same programs.
steps.why: They share the same instruction set architecture (for example x86-64) but are organized differently inside.

steps.title: Four building blocks

nodes.label: CPU
nodes.note: The **CPU** fetches instructions and carries them out.
nodes.example: The processor chip in your laptop or phone.

nodes.label: Memory
nodes.note: **Memory** holds the running program and its data. It is fast, but loses its contents when power is off.
nodes.example: The RAM sticks in a laptop.

nodes.label: I/O devices
nodes.note: **Input/output** devices connect the computer to people and other machines.
nodes.example: A keyboard, a screen, an SSD or a Wi-Fi chip.

nodes.label: Interconnect
nodes.note: The **interconnect** (buses) carries signals between all the other parts.
nodes.example: The wiring on the motherboard that joins everything.

steps.why: These four blocks appear in every device you own, from a smartwatch to a data-center server.

explainAgain.beginner: Think of a kitchen: the cook is the CPU, the counter is memory, the doors and windows are I/O, and the people carrying plates are the interconnect.

notes.explain: Click each box as you introduce it.
misconceptions: Students call the whole computer 'the CPU'.

steps.real: Every smartphone, laptop, game console and car computer is built from these same four blocks.

mistake.wrong: Memory and storage are the same thing.
mistake.right: Memory (RAM) holds what is running now and loses its contents without power. Storage (SSD or disk) keeps files permanently.
mistake.why: Programs are copied from storage into memory before the CPU runs them.

steps.title: The stored-program idea

nodes.label: Input
nodes.note: Programs and data come in from an input device.

nodes.label: Memory
nodes.note: Both the program and its data are kept here. This is the **stored-program** idea (von Neumann).

nodes.label: CPU
nodes.note: The CPU fetches instructions and data from memory and works on them.

nodes.label: Output
nodes.note: Results are sent to an output device.

steps.why: Because programs are just data in memory, a computer can load a brand-new program without being rewired.

deeper.text: In a **Harvard** architecture, instructions and data use separate memories. Most modern CPUs mix both ideas, using separate instruction and data caches on top of one main memory.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each component with its job.

pairs.b: Holds the running program and data
Connect the computer to the outside world

steps.why: Each block has one clear job, and they work together.

questions.q: What is the difference between architecture and organization?
questions.a: Architecture is what the programmer sees (what the computer can do). Organization is how the hardware implements it.

questions.q: Name the four main building blocks of a computer.
questions.a: CPU, memory, input/output devices and the interconnect (buses).
Instructions and data are both kept in memory, so a new program can be loaded without rewiring the machine.

steps.title: Three buses, three jobs

nodes.label: Address bus
nodes.note: Carries the **address** of the memory location or device. It flows one way, from the CPU outwards.

nodes.label: Data bus
nodes.note: Carries the actual **data** being read or written. It flows in both directions.

nodes.label: Control bus
nodes.note: Carries signals such as **read**, **write** and the clock.

steps.why: The width of these buses limits how much memory a computer can address and how much data moves at once.

explainAgain.beginner: To ask a friend for a book: the address bus is the shelf number, the data bus is the book being handed over, and the control bus is the word "please give" or "please put back".

deeper.text: A bus with *n* address lines can name 2^n different locations. A 32-bit address bus can address 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 bytes, which is 4 GiB.

steps.real: The slots for RAM and for a graphics card on a motherboard, and the USB port you plug devices into, are all buses carrying addresses, data and control signals.

mistake.wrong: The data bus carries the address.
mistake.right: The address bus carries the address. The data bus carries the value.

notes.explain: Keep this short: buses return in Class 22 (bandwidth, reliability, RAID). Only the three jobs matter today.

steps.question: The CPU wants the value stored at memory address `0x2000`. Which bus carries the address `0x2000`?

nodes.label: CPU puts 0x2000 on the address bus
nodes.note: The address bus names the memory location.

nodes.label: CPU asserts READ on the control bus
nodes.note: The control bus says what to do.

nodes.label: Memory puts the value on the data bus
nodes.note: The data bus carries the value back.

nodes.label: CPU copies the value into a register
nodes.note: The read is complete.

steps.result: The address goes out on the address bus; the answer comes back on the data bus.

steps.title: Below your program: from code to hardware

nodes.label: High-level program
nodes.note: People write programs in a language close to how they think.

nodes.label: Compiler
nodes.note: A **compiler** translates the high-level program into assembly language for one particular ISA.

nodes.label: Assembly language
nodes.note: Assembly is a human-readable form of machine instructions.

nodes.label: Assembler
nodes.note: An **assembler** turns each assembly instruction into binary.

nodes.label: Machine code
nodes.note: The CPU only understands patterns of 0s and 1s.

nodes.label: Hardware
nodes.note: The processor fetches the binary instructions and carries them out.

steps.why: Software and hardware speak different languages, and these layers translate between them. This is the software/hardware interface.
steps.real: When you install an app, you are installing machine code built for your phone's or laptop's instruction set.

mistake.wrong: The CPU runs C or Java directly.
mistake.right: The CPU only runs machine code. Compilers and assemblers (or an interpreter) translate for it.

explainAgain.beginner: It is like translating a recipe from English into the exact button presses of a kitchen robot. Each step makes it less human and more machine.
explainAgain.technical: A compiler lowers high-level code to the target ISA's assembly; an assembler encodes it into machine words; the processor decodes and executes those words.

notes.explain: Click each stage. The MIPS example previews Classes 5 to 7; students need not decode the binary today.
misconceptions: Students think the CPU understands the programming language.

steps.title: Instruction execution: the big picture

nodes.label: Fetch
nodes.note: The CPU uses the **program counter** (PC) as an address and reads the next instruction from memory.
nodes.example: The PC holds the address of the instruction to run.

nodes.label: Decode
nodes.note: The control unit decodes the instruction and reads the registers it names.

nodes.label: Execute
nodes.note: The ALU computes the result, or the address for a memory access.

nodes.label: Write result
nodes.note: The result goes to a register (or memory) and the PC moves on to the next instruction.
nodes.example: For add $s0, $s1, $s2 the sum is written to $s0.

steps.why: Every instruction of every program goes through this same loop, billions of times a second.
steps.real: Whenever your phone is awake, its processor is running this fetch, decode, execute loop.

notes.explain: This is only an overview. Classes 10 and 11 build the real datapath step by step.

steps.question: Every MIPS instruction is 4 bytes long. The CPU has just fetched the instruction at address 100. Normally, which address will the program counter hold for the next instruction?
steps.result: Each instruction is 4 bytes, so the next one is 4 bytes further on, unless a branch or jump changes the PC.

steps.question: Which program turns assembly language into binary machine code?
steps.why: The assembler encodes each assembly instruction as binary machine code.
feedback: The compiler translates a high-level language such as C into assembly language.
The operating system manages programs and resources; it does not translate code.
Memory only stores the machine code.

steps.title: Design goals

head: Goal
The question
How it is measured
rows: How fast does it run programs?
What does it cost to build and buy?
How much energy and heat does it use?

steps.why: Improving one goal usually costs another, so architects balance all four for a purpose.
steps.real: A phone favors low power, a server favors performance and reliability, and a toy favors low cost.

mistake.wrong: The best computer is simply the fastest one.
mistake.right: Best depends on the balance of performance, cost, power and reliability for the job.

notes.explain: Class 2 and 3 take performance, cost and power further; reliability returns in Class 22.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each design goal with how it is measured.
steps.why: Each goal has its own measure, and architects trade them against each other.

steps.title: What does a computer architect do?

items: Decides **what** the computer can do (the instruction set)
Decides **how** it is built (CPU, caches, memory, buses)
Keeps old software working on new hardware

steps.why: The chip in your phone, the servers behind a website and the processor training an AI model all come from an architect's trade-offs.

notes.explain: Stress the word *balance*: there is no perfect chip, only the best compromise for a purpose.
notes.ask: Would a smartwatch chip and a supercomputer chip make the same trade-offs? Why not?
misconceptions: Students think architects only design buildings, or only design the chip's circuits.

steps.real: The processors in phones, laptops, data centers and AI accelerators all come from architecture teams making these trade-offs for different goals.

steps.title: Eight great ideas in computer architecture

nodes.label: Design for Moore's law
nodes.sub: aim at where technology will be
nodes.note: Technology improves so quickly that a design must target the technology available when the product ships, not today's.

nodes.label: Use abstraction
nodes.note: Layers with simple interfaces let each layer be designed without knowing the layers around it.

nodes.label: Make the common case fast
nodes.note: Speeding up the frequent case helps more, and is usually easier, than speeding up a rare one.

nodes.label: Performance via parallelism
nodes.note: Doing operations at the same time gives more work per second.

nodes.label: Performance via pipelining
nodes.note: Like an assembly line, a pipeline works on different stages of several tasks at once.

nodes.label: Performance via prediction
nodes.note: If a good guess is cheaper than waiting, start the likely work early and recover when the guess is wrong.

nodes.label: Hierarchy of memories
nodes.sub: small and fast to big and slow
nodes.note: Keep fast, small, expensive memory near the processor and large, slow, cheap memory further away.

nodes.label: Dependability via redundancy
nodes.note: Extra components let a system keep working when one part fails.

steps.why: These eight ideas come back in almost every lesson of this course. Each later topic is one or more of them in detail.
steps.real: A phone's cache is the hierarchy of memories, its many cores use parallelism, and a data center keeps working through a disk failure because of redundancy.

explainAgain.beginner: They are eight habits good computer designers use: plan for fast change, hide detail, speed up the common case, do things together, overlap steps, guess ahead, keep things close, and have spares.

deeper.text: Pipelining, prediction and the memory hierarchy each get their own lessons later in the course, so treat today as a map of the territory.

notes.explain: Click each idea and ask which everyday system uses it. The names are the textbook's; the explanations here are our own.

steps.question: A cache keeps recently used data close to the CPU so it can be reached quickly. Which great idea does this illustrate?
steps.why: Keeping a small, fast memory near the processor in front of a large, slow one is the hierarchy of memories.
feedback: Pipelining overlaps the steps of different instructions. A cache is about where data is kept.
Redundancy adds spare parts for reliability, not speed.
Prediction guesses an outcome and starts early. A cache stores data that was already used.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Why can the same program run on an Intel processor and an AMD processor even though their insides are different?
steps.answer: Both implement the same instruction set architecture (x86-64). A program depends only on the ISA, so different organizations can run it.

notes.explain: Walk around and listen for the words *same instruction set*.
notes.discuss: What happens to a program built for an ARM phone if you try to run it on an x86 laptop?

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: Should a smartwatch and a supercomputer follow the same architecture? Discuss.
ideas: They can share an instruction set, but their organizations will look very different.
A smartwatch optimizes battery life and size.
A supercomputer optimizes total throughput and uses thousands of chips.
Architecture is the contract; organization adapts to the goal.

notes.explain: Let the timer run, then reveal the key ideas one at a time and match them to what students said.
notes.discuss: Which goal would force a different instruction set, and which only a different organization?

steps.question: Name the four main building blocks of a computer.
steps.answer: CPU, memory, input/output devices and the interconnect (buses).
steps.solution: The CPU executes instructions, memory holds programs and data, I/O devices connect to the outside world, and the buses carry signals between them.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement below is wrong. Click it.
lines: 2. Main memory keeps its contents when the power is turned off.
3. I/O devices connect the computer to the outside world.
4. Buses carry signals between the components.
steps.explain: Main memory (RAM) is volatile: it loses its contents without power. Disks and SSDs keep data.
steps.fix: Main memory loses its contents when power is off.

steps.question:
Is each design decision about *architecture* or *organization*?
(a) Adding a new instruction that adds two vectors
(b) Making the multiplier use a faster circuit
(c) Choosing 64-bit registers that programs can use
(d) Adding a bigger cache
steps.hint: Ask: can a programmer see this change in the instructions or registers they use?
steps.solution:
(a) A new instruction is visible to programmers, so it is architecture.
(b) A faster circuit changes how multiply is done, not what programmers see, so it is organization.
(c) Register size is visible to programs, so it is architecture.
(d) A cache is transparent to programs, so it is organization.

steps.question: A company wants a new chip that is twice as fast but must still run every program its customers already own. Which kind of change is safest, and what must they avoid changing?
steps.hint: Which layer do existing programs depend on?
steps.answer: Change the organization (deeper pipelines, bigger caches, faster circuits). Keep the instruction set architecture the same.
steps.solution: Existing programs depend only on the ISA. Improving the organization makes the same instructions run faster without breaking anything. New instructions can be added, but removing or changing existing ones would break old software.

steps.title: Exam practice: numerical
steps.question: A processor has a 24-bit address bus and addresses one byte per address. What is the largest memory it can address?
steps.hint: Each extra address line doubles the number of addresses.
steps.solution:
With n address lines there are 2^n different addresses.
2^24 = 16,777,216.
At one byte per address that is 16,777,216 bytes = 16 × 1,048,576 = 16 MiB.
steps.mistake: Writing 24 × 8 or 24² instead of 2 raised to the power 24.

steps.title: Exam practice: short answer
steps.question: In two or three sentences, explain the difference between computer architecture and computer organization. Give one example of each.
steps.answer: Architecture is the programmer-visible design: instruction set, registers, addressing modes. Organization is how it is implemented in hardware: datapath, caches, buses. Example: having an ADD instruction is architecture; building it with a fast adder circuit is organization.
steps.solution: A good answer names both ideas, says who sees each one (programmer versus hardware designer) and gives an example on each side.
steps.mistake: Using the two words as if they meant the same thing, or describing only hardware.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Put the journey from a program to the hardware in order.
items: Write the program in C or Java
The assembler produces binary machine code
The CPU fetches and executes the instructions
steps.why: Each layer feeds the next: the program becomes assembly, assembly becomes binary, and binary is what the hardware runs.

steps.title: What you should remember
remember: Architecture is what the programmer sees; organization is how it is built.
A computer has a CPU, memory, I/O devices and an interconnect (buses).
Programs become machine instructions through a compiler and an assembler.
Every instruction is fetched, decoded, executed and its result written.
The four design goals are performance, cost, power and reliability, and they trade against each other.
An architect balances them for a purpose and keeps old software working.

mistakes.wrong: Architecture and organization mean the same thing.
mistakes.right: Architecture is what the programmer sees; organization is how it is built.

mistakes.wrong: The data bus carries the address.
mistakes.right: The address bus carries the address; the data bus carries the value.

mistakes.wrong: A faster chip always needs a new instruction set.
mistakes.right: A new organization can run the same ISA faster.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: Computer architecture is the design of a computer as the programmer sees it, while organization is how the hardware builds it. A computer has a CPU, memory, I/O devices and an interconnect. Programs and data live together in memory. The address, data and control buses move information between parts. Architects balance performance, cost and power while keeping old software working.

questions.question: Which describes computer *architecture*?
options: The attributes of a computer that a programmer can see
The materials used to make the chip
How the hardware is wired inside
The size of the computer case
questions.why: Architecture is the programmer-visible behavior of the machine.
questions.misconception: How the hardware is wired inside is organization, not architecture.

questions.statement: Memory holds both the running program and its data.
questions.misconception: Programs are kept in memory just like data.

questions.question: Which component carries out instructions?
questions.why: The CPU fetches and executes instructions.
questions.misconception: Memory stores them and buses carry signals; neither executes anything.

questions.question: Which bus carries the memory address from the CPU?
questions.why: The address bus names the memory location.
questions.misconception: The data bus carries the value, and the control bus carries signals such as READ.

questions.question: A 20-bit address bus can address how many locations?
questions.misconception: Each extra address line doubles the number of locations, so the count is 2 raised to the number of lines.

questions.question: Adding a bigger cache without changing what programmers can see is a change to the…
questions.why: A cache is invisible to programs, so it is an organization change.
questions.misconception: Architecture covers only what programs can see and use.

questions.question: Why can one program run on processors from different companies?
options: They are built from the same materials
They implement the same instruction set architecture
The program contains its own CPU
questions.why: Programs depend only on the ISA, not on how the chip is built.
questions.misconception: Different companies usually have different internal designs; the shared part is the ISA.

questions.question: The CPU writes the value 7 to address 0x10. Which line is correct?
options: Address bus: 7, Data bus: 0x10, Control: WRITE
Address bus: 0x10, Data bus: 7, Control: WRITE
Address bus: 0x10, Data bus: 7, Control: READ
Address bus: WRITE, Data bus: 0x10, Control: 7
questions.why: The address bus carries the location, the data bus the value, and the control bus the operation.
questions.misconception: Keep the three jobs straight: where, what, and how.

questions.question: A maker plans a new processor generation. Which change would force customers to rewrite or recompile existing programs?
options: Removing instructions that programs already use
Adding more bus lines between the CPU and memory
questions.why: Removing instructions changes the architecture, so old programs may no longer run.
questions.misconception: Caches, manufacturing and bus width are organization or technology changes that old programs never notice.

items.q: What is the difference between architecture and organization?
items.a: Architecture is what the programmer sees; organization is how the hardware implements it.

items.q: Name the three buses and what each carries.
items.a: Address bus: the location. Data bus: the value. Control bus: signals such as read, write and clock.
Instructions and data are both stored in memory.

items.q: What does a computer architect balance?
items.a: Performance, cost and power, while keeping old software working.
